{{Short description|American chemist (born 1964)}}
'''James Lincoln Leighton''' (born February 12, 1964) is an American chemist. He is a professor of chemistry in the Department of Chemistry at [[Columbia University]]. He is known for his non-[[aldol reaction|aldol]] approaches to [[polyketide]]s.

== Education and career ==

Leighton was born in [[New Haven, Connecticut]]. As an undergraduate at [[Yale University]] (B.S. 1987), Leighton worked for synthetic chemist [[Samuel J. Danishefsky]]. After 2 years with Merck Research Laboratories, Leighton began his graduate studies with Abbott and James Lawrence Professor [[David A. Evans]] at [[Harvard University]] (Ph.D. 1994), culminating in the total syntheses of both [[Calyculin]] A <ref>Total synthesis of (+)-calyculin A. ''J. Am. Chem. Soc.'' '''1992''', ''114'', 9434-9453 {{doi|10.1021/ja00050a024}}</ref> and [[Zaragozic acid]].<ref>Asymmetric Synthesis of the Squalene Synthase Inhibitor Zaragozic Acid C. ''J. Am. Chem. Soc.'' '''1994''', ''116'', 12111-12112 {{doi|10.1021/ja00105a085}}</ref> Leighton continued his chemical studies as an [[National Science Foundation|NSF]] postdoctoral fellow with Sheldon Emery Professor [[Eric Jacobsen (chemist)|Eric N. Jacobsen]], also of Harvard University, developing initial methods for what became known as the Jacobsen hydrolytic kinetic resolution.

In 1996, Leighton began his independent career at Columbia, becoming a full professor in 2004. In recognition of his scholarly contributions in the laboratory and classroom, he was awarded the [[Arthur C. Cope]] Scholar award (2003) by the [[American Chemical Society]],<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/arthur-c-cope-scholar-awards.html |title="ACS Cope Award" |access-date=2015-04-06 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304115720/http://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/arthur-c-cope-scholar-awards.html |archive-date=2016-03-04 |url-status=dead }}</ref> as well as the [[Mark Van Doren]] Award for Teaching, Columbia's most prestigious teaching award.<ref>Mark Van Doren Award for Teaching. http://www.columbia.edu/cu/vpas/about/recognition.html#2</ref>

==Notable contributions==
In addition to Leighton's novel methods for synthesizing natural products, including: CP-263,114,<ref>An Approach to the Synthesis of CP-263,114:  A Remarkably Facile Silyloxy-Cope Rearrangement. ''J. Am. Chem. Soc.'' '''1999''', ''121'', 890-891. {{doi|10.1021/ja983609x}}</ref> Leucascandrolide A,<ref>Total Synthesis of Leucascandrolide A. ''J. Am. Chem. Soc.'' '''2000''', ''122'', 12894-12895. {{doi|10.1021/ja003593m}}</ref> Mycoticin A,<ref>Formal Total Synthesis of Mycoticin A. ''J. Am. Chem. Soc.'' '''2001''', ''123'', 341-342. {{doi|10.1021/ja0035102}}</ref> SCH 351448,<ref>{{Cite web |last=and |first=Sergei Bolshakov |last2=Leighton* |first2=James L. |date=2005-07-20 |title=Efficient Asymmetric Synthesis of (+)-SCH 351448 |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/pdf/10.1021/ol0515006 |access-date=2025-09-30 |website=ACS Publications |language=en |doi=10.1021/ol0515006 |pmc=1393291 |pmid=16092881}}</ref> Dolabelide D,<ref>Total Synthesis of Dolabelide D. ''J. Am. Chem. Soc.'' '''2006''', ''128'', 2796-2797. {{doi|10.1021/ja058692k}}</ref> Manzacidin C,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Tran |first=Kristy |last2=Lombardi |first2=Pamela J. |last3=Leighton |first3=James L. |date=2008-07-17 |title=An Efficient Asymmetric Synthesis of Manzacidin C |url=https://doi.org/10.1021/ol8011869 |journal=Organic Letters |volume=10 |issue=14 |pages=3165–3167 |doi=10.1021/ol8011869 |issn=1523-7060|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Zincophorin, he has also pioneered the concept of strain-release silane [[Lewis acids]].<ref>Origins of Stereoselectivity in Strain-Release Allylations. ''Angew. Chem. Int. Ed.'' '''2004''', ''44'', 938-941. {{doi|10.1002/anie.200462130}}</ref> In particular, he has developed a silicon/[[pseudoephedrine]] allylation reagent for the highly enantioselective allylation of aldehydes and aldehyde/ketone derived [[hydrazones]] to give chiral alcohols and secondary/tertiary carbinamines, respectively.
